title: Signal or noise?
task: Say whether this is a real signal, and what on the desk decides it.
scene: Seven patients across three hospitals in four days, with the same four symptoms. Dr. Sofia Morales has the printouts, and the press office has asked twice whether to say anything.
question: The city normally sees about two of these a year. How many were there in four days?
takeaway: A count becomes a signal only when something says what was expected instead.
why: A count on its own is not a signal. What makes it one is a comparison with what was expected, written down beforehand. This city logs about two of these a year. Seven in four days is not a busy week.
answerText: A real signal. Two a year is what this city normally sees. And two of the seven were found a second way.

choices: A real jump above what this city normally sees.
Something the shared alert rule created by itself.
Ordinary autumn coughs and colds.
Impossible to say, because nobody knows how many people are out there.
choiceMechanisms: Seven in four days, against about two a year, is far outside what the system normally does.
Every case was found the same way, by the same rule.
This kind of illness is common in autumn, and seven is inside the usual wobble.
Seven is a count with nothing underneath it.
rebuttals: The alert rule is the right worry, and it is the one this panel rules out. Five came through it and two did not.
Autumn coughs would lift the other illnesses too. Those are flat, so whatever this is, it is not the season.
The population figures are on the desk. All three hospitals supplied theirs, so that objection has already been answered.
text.headline: Seven cases in four days, against a thing the city normally logs twice a year.

title: What counts as a case
task: Put the four steps in the order each one can be checked in.
scene: Three hospitals start counting at six in the morning. Each has written its own idea of what counts. Dr. Lena Ortiz, who leads the ward side, wants one on every desk before the night shift leaves.
takeaway: A definition turns a worry into something two people can count the same way.
why: A definition of what counts is an instrument, and it can be wrong in two directions. Too narrow and most of the spread is invisible. Too wide and the count fills up with ordinary autumn coughs. That is why it gets tested twice before it goes out.

rebuttals: The notes come first. What these patients share has to come out of the patients, not out of the drafting.
Symptoms, timing and place next, because that is what somebody actually applies at four in the morning.
Testing before it goes out, not after. Known cases catch a definition that is too narrow, and obvious non-cases catch one that is too wide.
The revision date goes out with it. Without one, three hospitals keep counting to a definition everybody knows is temporary.
cards: Read the notes of the patients already in.
Write the symptoms, timing and place plainly enough to use.
Try it on known cases, and on clear non-cases.
Send it out with a date to revise it.

title: Spend the first afternoon
task: Make the outbreak-response call before the next case report arrives.
scene: Morales can start one thing this afternoon. Four are ready to go, and tomorrow's hospital numbers will land before any second one can start.
question: Three hospitals are sending numbers tomorrow. What has to be the same before they can be added together?
takeaway: The best first measurement is the one that makes everything measured later comparable.
why: Three hospitals are about to send in three sets of numbers. They can only be added together if the same rule made them. A shared list, with the same dates and the same town figures, is what does that.
answerText: Start the shared list. Tomorrow's three counts only become one usable picture if the same definition and the same dates made them.

choices: The rule for what counts as a case
The name of the doctor who reported it
The hospital each patient arrived at
The time of day the count was made
rebuttals: Who reported it is worth recording and changes no count.
Which hospital they went to is the thing being compared, not fixed.
The hour of the count matters far less than what was counted.

title: What kind of germ fits everything?
task: Say which explanation fits every reading, including the quiet ones.
scene: Pathology has four results from the same samples and still cannot name what this is. The samples are waiting under the hood. Ortiz needs a broad answer before the overnight run is booked.
question: Bacteria and fungi are cells. Nothing cell-shaped is on the slide. What does that rule out?
takeaway: What something is gets settled by several tests together, not by one striking picture.
why: The negative results do most of the work. Nothing cell-shaped is visible. The marker that finds bacteria is absent. The stain built to find fungal walls is clean, and it rarely misses. The signal only grows where there are living cells to grow in, which fits something that cannot copy itself alone.
answerText: Something virus-like. Three separate looks for a cell came back empty, and it only copies itself inside living cells.

choices: Something virus-like.
A bacterium of some kind.
A fungus of some kind.
Something that got in from the laboratory.
choiceMechanisms: Not a cell of its own, and it can only copy itself inside a living cell.
A cell in its own right, which would leave the markers and shapes of one.
A cell with a wall, which is exactly what the stain is built to find.
Stray material loose in the room, rather than anything in the patients.
rebuttals: A bacterium is a cell, and it would leave something behind. Three separate looks came back empty.
A fungus would show its wall on a stain built to find it. That stain is clean, and it rarely misses.
Something from the room is the right suspicion, and the blank is how it gets checked. This blank is clean.
text.headline: Several clues from the same samples, and no name yet.

equations.e: how many after n rounds = start × 2 each round
equations.about: why an outbreak grows so fast

title: From sample to a first answer
task: Put the four steps in the order they have to happen.
scene: The bench has patient material, healthy tissue and a blank on it. There are four things it could do with them, and two of them use up what they measure.
takeaway: A first answer is built out of several observations, not printed by one machine.
why: Each step only means something if the step before it held. The blank and the healthy tissue come first, because they separate the germ from whatever it arrived in. Measure a shape in a dirty sample and you have measured the dirt, close up.

rebuttals: The controls come first, because everything after them is a claim about the patient rather than the tube.
Shape before behaviour. Whether something needs a living cell is a question about an organism, and you do not have one yet.
The copying question comes third. It is the slowest and the fussiest, and worth running only on something the first two steps survived.
Putting it together comes last. A first answer is what the other three produce, not a step on its own.
cards: Compare the patient material against healthy tissue and a blank.
Look at its size, its coat and its genetic material.
Ask whether it can copy itself without a cell.
Put the separate observations together into a first answer.

title: When heat changes the test
task: Say what the temperature comparison shows.
scene: A test works after being warmed to thirty-seven degrees. After the same part is held at fifty-five, it mostly stops working. Nothing else was changed.
question: What does the temperature comparison show?
takeaway: Change one thing and hold the rest, and what changes belongs to the thing you changed.
why: Warming things up usually speeds a reaction up. Everything moves about more and bumps into more. That only holds while the working part keeps its shape. Push the heat far enough and the shape goes, and so does the pocket where the work happens.
answerText: The heat wrecked the shape of the working part. Everything else was held the same, so the loss belongs to the temperature.

choices: The higher temperature wrecked the shape the test depends on.
More heat always means faster, so it ran too fast.
The patient's sample went off before it was tested.
The thing being looked for was destroyed at fifty-five degrees.
rebuttals: Heat speeds a reaction only while the working part is still working. Its shape sets the limit.
What changed here is the temperature the working part was held at, not the patient sample.
This test measures whether the working part still works. It says nothing about the target being destroyed.

title: Getting into a cell
task: Put the four steps of getting in into order.
scene: Only some kinds of cell in the airway are affected. The culture wing has four cards about getting into a cell, and nobody has put them in order.
takeaway: A cell's outside decides what can get in, which is why only some cells are affected.
why: The order is physical, and it explains the pattern. Nothing gets in until something on the surface is recognised. A cell without the right piece on its outside cannot be entered, however much lands on it. The layer bends next, because that is what the recognition sets off. Material crosses after that.

rebuttals: Recognition first. It decides which cells are even candidates, which is why some kinds are affected and others are not.
The layer bends because something bound to it. That is a consequence of recognition rather than a step on its own.
Material crosses only after the layer has rearranged. That is what the rearranging is for.
The hijacked machinery is last, because it is an effect. A cell doing the wrong work has already been entered.
cards: A piece on the cell surface recognises the germ.
The cell's outer layer bends, or joins with it.
The material crosses into the cell.
The cell's own machinery starts being used for something else.

title: Which way things cross
task: Match each observation to how the material is crossing.
scene: Four things from the culture bench, each about something crossing a cell's outer layer. The cell biologist wants each one named before the model goes further.
takeaway: How something crosses is worked out from the rules it obeys, not from what it is called.
why: Three things tell these apart, and none of them is the name of the molecule. Which way it goes. Downhill is free, uphill costs, and the energy spent is the receipt. Whether it needs help. Something small and greasy slips through, and a charged particle cannot. And how big it is.

choices: Straight through the layer, with no help.
Through a doorway, still downhill and still free.
Pushed uphill, which is what the energy is for.
Wrapped up and swallowed whole.
rebuttals: Downhill and needing no help is the simplest case. It is small and greasy enough to cross the layer itself.
Downhill through a doorway is still free. The doorway supplies the choosiness, not the push.
Uphill with energy spent is the one where the cell is doing work, and the cost is what identifies it.
Something large being wrapped up is a different process from anything crossing the layer.
scenarios: Something small and greasy drifts from more to less.
A charged particle goes the same way, through a doorway.
Something is moved uphill, and energy gets spent doing it.
Something large is wrapped up by the layer and taken in.

title: Separate landing from getting in
task: Change one thing at a time, then put it back, and say whether the landing step is required.
scene: Dr. Maya Chen has a test that counts how much gets into airway cells. Three changes are ready to try, and the treatment meeting needs to know about the first step.
question: Which single change makes the entry follow the landing step rather than the dose or the handling?
takeaway: A cause is proved when changing one thing changes the result, and putting it back brings it back.
why: Counting the landing places on a cell is only a clue. The real test asks whether the landing step is needed. Block it, keep the dose and the handling the same, and what gets in falls hard. Add a look-alike blocker and nothing changes, so it was not just adding something.
answerText: Blocking the landing step. Entry falls from about 100 to 22, and washing the blocker off brings it back to 96. The look-alike blocker changes nothing.

control.dataProvenance: invented simulated, non-infectious classroom fluorescence values; mechanism is source-derived
control.hint: Keep two controls fixed while changing the third. A useful cause should move the entry signal when changed and restore it when reversed.

shape.dataProvenance: invented simulated, non-infectious classroom fluorescence values; mechanism is source-derived
shape.hint: Keep two controls fixed while changing the third. A useful cause should move the entry signal when changed and restore it when reversed.

title: A run you can trust by morning
task: Put the four steps of the run in order.
scene: Hospitals want a test by sunrise and the room has four hours. Four steps are on the whiteboard. The machine multiplies whatever is in the tube a billion times, which is why the order is argued about.
takeaway: A test result is what a controlled process produced, not what a machine displayed.
why: A patient result read before the controls is a machine reading, not evidence. The name has to survive the first step, or the answer belongs to nobody. The controls go in with the samples. Added later, they test a different run. One shows the chemistry worked.

rebuttals: Extraction first, with the name attached. A result that cannot be tied to a patient is nobody's diagnosis.
The controls go in with the samples. Added afterwards, they test a different run from the one that gave the result.
The copying comes third. It is the step everything else exists to make readable.
Reading last, and only on condition. If a control misbehaved, the patient tubes cannot be read however clean they look.
cards: Get the material out of the sample, without losing whose it is.
Put the controls into the run, alongside the samples.
Run the copying, with settings somebody has checked.
Read the patient's result, but only if the controls behaved.

title: Why did the test turn positive?
task: Open what each result depends on, keep what stands, and name what the rest share.
scene: Dr. Ravi Patel has patient tubes, two controls and a separate machine on one screen. One ward has already cleared isolation rooms. If this run is wrong, patients get moved before morning.
question: Which results share one path, and what evidence survives it?
takeaway: Agreement is not evidence when everything agreeing came down the same pipe.
why: A blank tube has no patient material in it. So a positive there came from the room or the chemicals. The patient tubes went through the same room and the same chemicals. That makes their positives doubtful, however many there are.
answerText: The patient tubes and the blank share one run, so stray material explains both. Keep the other machine's result.

text.headline: The overnight amplification run flags several patient samples as positive, but one control is also behaving strangely.

trace.hint: Do not count how many wells came up positive. Open what each result went through, keep the evidence that took a different path, and then name what the rest have in common.

channels.label: The blank tube, with no patient sample in it
The tube that is meant to be positive
channels.reading: came up positive, as it should

channels.label: The same patients, on the other machine

resources.label: Stray copies loose in this run
The other machine and its own chemicals

shape.hint: Do not count how many wells came up positive. Open what each result went through, keep the evidence that took a different path, and then name what the rest have in common.

title: Four test cards, two ways to be wrong
task: Match each test card to what actually happened.
scene: Dr. Ravi Patel, the molecular diagnostics lead, gives you four sealed test cards. Each card shows the test result and the later confirmed truth. Your job is to learn the two different ways a test can be wrong.
takeaway: A test can miss a real case or flag someone who is not sick.
why: Tests are useful, but no test is perfect. A false negative misses a real case. A false positive flags someone who is not a case. Knowing both kinds of mistake helps the town decide when to repeat a test or use a second method.
answerText: The two mistakes are false positive and false negative; they mean different things and lead to different follow-up actions.

text.setup: Drag each card to its name.
choices: True positive
False positive
True negative
False negative
rebuttals: The test said positive and the person really was a case.
The test said positive but the person was not a case.
The test said negative and the person really was not a case.
The test said negative but the person really was a case.
scenarios: Positive test; later confirmed sick
Positive test; later confirmed not sick
Negative test; later confirmed not sick
Negative test; later confirmed sick

title: Where the oxygen stops getting through
task: Build the path oxygen takes, then name the step that is holding it up.
scene: A patient's oxygen is dropping while Dr. Lena Ortiz reads the bedside screen. The blood carries plenty. The heart is pumping normally. The new lung pictures are not normal at all.
question: Where is the oxygen path most likely failing?
takeaway: A chain is found by checking every handover, and the normal ones narrow it down as much as the odd ones.
why: Oxygen delivery is a chain, so one normal reading proves nothing on its own. The breathing out is near normal, so the patient is not simply under-breathing. The blood carries a normal amount, so there is no shortage of carriers.
answerText: The handover from air into blood, in the lungs. Breathing, carrying and pumping all read normal, and the lung pictures do not.

text.headline: Two patients have severe fatigue and low tissue oxygen delivery.

chain.hint: Build the route oxygen must follow. Then use each reading to ask which link is still compatible with the failure; the largest number on the screen is not automatically the governing one.

links.label: Ventilation to the alveoli
links.transfers: fresh gas from the airways to the alveoli

links.label: Air–blood gas exchange
links.reading: arterial oxygen low; diffuse alveolar involvement on imaging

links.label: Cardiac flow
links.transfers: oxygenated blood through the systemic circulation

links.label: Tissue delivery and use
links.transfers: oxygen from capillary blood to cells
links.reading: downstream metabolic evidence not yet complete

shape.hint: Build the route oxygen must follow. Then use each reading to ask which link is still compatible with the failure; the largest number on the screen is not automatically the governing one.

title: Follow the oxygen
task: Put the oxygen path in order, then find the bottleneck.
scene: Dr. Lena Ortiz, the clinical physiology lead, has one patient whose blood contains oxygen but whose body is still not getting enough. Build the path oxygen must travel from the room to the tissues.
question: Which link can fail even when the blood itself is carrying oxygen?
takeaway: Getting oxygen into blood is only part of the job. The body also needs blood to move it to the tissues.
why: Oxygen has to cross several links: air, lungs, blood, pumping heart, then tissues. If the blood is carrying oxygen but the heart is not moving enough blood, delivery still falls. Following the chain helps locate the problem.
answerText: The pumping step is the bottleneck in this case.

text.headline: The oxygen number in the blood looks acceptable, but the patient is still struggling.

chain.hint: Put the links in physical order. Then use the clue to choose the link that is not moving enough oxygen onward.

shape.hint: Put the oxygen path in order and find the weak link.

title: Which measurement is still missing
task: Make the outbreak-response call before the next case report arrives.
scene: The oxygen path points at the lungs, and the team wants one more measurement before rounds. Three of the four on offer have already been taken, in one form or another.
question: Which measurement would actually add something here?
takeaway: The measurement worth taking is the one nobody can already answer from the chart.
why: Three of these have already been answered. The oxygen and carbon dioxide are on the chart from the last panel. The pump has been measured and read normal. Three machines agreeing about the same number tells you the machines agree, which nobody doubted.
answerText: What the tissues themselves show. Everything else on the list has already been measured, or repeats a number nobody is arguing about.

choices: What the body's tissues are showing downstream.
The oxygen and carbon dioxide in the blood.
How much blood the heart is moving.
The same blood-oxygen reading, on three machines.
rebuttals: The oxygen and carbon dioxide are already on the chart. Measuring them again is being precise about something nobody is arguing about.
The pump has been measured and read normal. Worth repeating if the patient changes, and it is not the missing measurement now.
Three machines agreeing tells you the machines agree. It does not add an observation.

title: What each stream is looking at
task: Match each stream to what it actually supports.
scene: Isolation has held for nine days and cases keep appearing. Four streams of information are on the table at the water plant, and each one saw a different slice of the city.
takeaway: Each stream watches a different group of people, and what it can show follows from which group.
why: Each of these watches a different set of people. The sewage watches everybody, whether or not they went to a hospital, which is why it can move first. It cannot name a person, and it does not prove the water is how anybody caught it.

choices: An early sign from the whole town, not a route.
Evidence that people can pass it on before they feel ill.
Volunteers at one station, who may not be typical.
Each patient takes weeks to recover, so the wards empty slowly.
rebuttals: Sewage can rise before hospitals do, because it watches everybody rather than the people who came in. It names nobody, and it does not prove the water is the route.
Exposures found before anybody felt ill say something about when it passes, from the only stream that asks people directly.
A volunteer sample at one station is a sample of volunteers at one station. The bias is in who agreed.
How many are on the wards and how many arrive today are different things, and this is how they come apart.
scenarios: The sewage reading rises before hospital admissions do.
Interviews at home find several exposures before people felt ill.
A survey at one station asks only people who volunteer.
The total on the wards stays high after new admissions fall.

title: Same body, different cell jobs
task: Match each cell type to the job it is built to do.
scene: Dr. Maya Chen, the cell biology lead, puts four cell pictures on the screen. They all come from one person, but they do not look or act the same. The germ seems able to attach to only one kind.
question: Why can a germ attach to one cell type but not another?
takeaway: Cells in the same body can have different shapes and surface parts because they do different jobs.
why: Your body is made of many kinds of cells. They share the same person, but they build different parts for different jobs. A germ that needs one particular surface part may attach well to one cell type and poorly to another.
answerText: Different cell types make different surface parts. The germ can attach where the matching surface part is present.

choices: Moves air and mucus
Carries oxygen
Contracts to pull
Forms a protective barrier
rebuttals: Airway cells help move material along the breathing passages.
Red blood cells are specialized for carrying oxygen.
Muscle cells are specialized for contraction.
Skin-like cells form protective barriers.

title: Carrier, carrier-of-it, or bystander
task: Match each pattern to the role it makes an animal.
scene: Sequences from three patients sit close to something found in animals along the river. The field station has four patterns on the board, and a trapper waiting outside with more animals.
takeaway: What an animal's role is comes from what it does over time, not from being close by.
why: A role is a claim about what keeps happening. It is not about which animal people are afraid of. Look for an animal that carries the germ a long time without getting very ill. That is where the germ lives between outbreaks.

choices: Where the germ lives between outbreaks.
Something that moves it about.
Where the chain stops.
Sharing the ground rather than the germ.
rebuttals: Carrying it a long time without much illness is what living with it looks like. It has to stay well enough to keep carrying.
A biting creature that moves it between animals is doing that job, whether or not the germ lives in it.
An animal that gets ill and passes it to nobody is a dead end. The chain arrives and stops there.
Common near cases and always clean is a shared habitat. Being nearby is the weakest evidence on the board.
scenarios: An animal carries it for a long time and hardly gets ill.
A biting creature moves it from one animal to another.
An animal gets ill, and passes it on to almost nobody.
An animal is common near cases and always tests clean.

title: Test where it lives
task: Put the four steps of the field campaign in order.
scene: Trappers report sick animals on the flood plain. Nobody has sampled in a way that could tell where the germ lives from an animal that caught it from people.
takeaway: A claim about where something lives needs a design that could have found it somewhere else.
why: One positive animal proves nothing about where a germ lives. What makes it evidence is a design that could have found it elsewhere and did not. So the order matters. Where people got ill says which animals to sample. Comparison places make the numbers mean something.

rebuttals: Cases against habitat first. That is what says which animals and which places are even candidates.
Even sampling, with comparison places, second. Find it only where you looked hardest and you have measured your own searching.
Comparing across animals and people third. It needs samples from both sides to compare.
Crossing over again and again comes last. One event can be a coincidence, and a claim about where a germ lives is a claim about something that keeps happening.
cards: Map where people got ill against where the animals live.
Sample the likely animals, and sample comparison places too.
Compare how common and how closely related, across both.
Test whether it explains the crossings happening again.

title: Choose the field campaign
task: Spend the twenty sampling slots so the campaign can tell the stories apart.
scene: Dr. Arjun Singh has one field campaign and twenty sampling slots. Likely animals, comparison places and a second visit later all want the same crews.
question: Which plan keeps the comparisons that could tell the stories apart?
takeaway: A field plan is defined by the explanations it can rule out with the samples it chooses.
why: A positive animal near a sick person fits several stories. The germ lives in that animal. It caught it from people. Or both met the same thing. Only comparisons can separate those. The same animal far from any cases tests the place. Other animals in the same habitat test the species.
answerText: Spread the slots across the likely animal near cases, the same animal far away, other animals nearby, and a second visit later.

allocate.hint: Every package buys a comparison and consumes field capacity. Keep the questions about geography, species and persistence answerable before spending anything on extra depth at one convenient site.

items.label: Existing human case locations and exposure histories
items.note: Already available; they guide sampling but do not establish an animal reservoir by themselves.

items.label: Same candidate species at comparison sites
Comparison species in the same habitats
Repeat sampling at a second time point
Extra dense sampling around one case household

shape.hint: Every package buys a comparison and consumes field capacity. Keep the questions about geography, species and persistence answerable before spending anything on extra depth at one convenient site.

title: Why did the treatment stop working?
task: Say which explanation fits the whole panel.
scene: A treatment that worked is failing, and another patient got worse overnight. The ward has the drug levels, the counts over time, and the germ's own readout from before and after.
question: Which explanation fits the whole panel?
takeaway: Something living can change while you watch, if what you are doing decides which ones survive.
why: Treatment can fail in several ways, and the normal readings say which. The drug reached the right level, and the count fell, so the drug was working and reaching its target.
answerText: The germ changed. The drug arrived, worked, and then stopped working while the changed form took over.

choices: The drug is not getting there.
The germ has changed, and the changed form took over.
It was the wrong germ all along.
Something got into the samples in the laboratory.
choiceMechanisms: The drug never reaches a level that does anything.
Treatment kills the ones it can, and the survivors take over.
The first answer was wrong, so the treatment never fitted.
The rise is a laboratory artefact rather than anything in the patient.
rebuttals: Not getting there means the drug never arrives. The level was measured, it was right, and the count fell to prove it.
The wrong germ would never have responded at all. This one fell before it came back.
Something loose in the laboratory would not spare the reference sample, which was run alongside and still responds.
text.headline: A treatment knocks the germ down, and then the counts climb again while the patient is still taking it.

title: How resistance spreads
task: Put the four steps in order.
scene: The treatment worked for six weeks, and now fails in one patient in four. The failures cluster on the wards where it has been used longest. Somebody has said the germ learned to beat it.
takeaway: Nothing learns. What changes is which ones leave descendants.
why: A treatment does not teach a germ anything, and it does not make the form it needs. That form was already there, rare, before the drug arrived. What the drug changes is which ones have offspring.

rebuttals: The rare ones exist first. This is the step that separates the real explanation from a story about a germ learning.
Treatment kills what it can. That is what choosing looks like, and it acts on what is already there.
The survivors multiply, which is how something rare stops being rare.
Being left with mostly the tough form is the outcome, and it is what the ward is now measuring.
cards: A few of them are already different, before any treatment.
The treatment clears the vulnerable ones far better.
The ones it cannot kill survive and multiply.
What is left is mostly the form the drug cannot touch.

title: One thing before the prescriptions change
task: Choose the one test to run before the treatment plan is rewritten.
scene: The treatment worked in eighty-two patients in a hundred nine weeks ago, and in fifty-one now. Eleven of the failures had their doses recorded and their drug levels checked.
question: What is the one thing to do before anybody's prescription changes?
takeaway: Compare the failures with matched successes, or the finding is just a description of the failures.
why: A treatment can fail in three places. It can be given wrongly, it can fail to arrive, or it can arrive and no longer work. Recorded doses and measured levels rule out the first two here. So the change is probably in the germ.
answerText: Read the germ from the failures and from matched patients who got better. The comparison is what makes it evidence.

choices: Read the germ from the failures, alongside matched patients who got better.
Measure how much drug each patient actually got.
Raise the dose for everybody on the ward.
Try different drugs and combinations, under a proper plan.
rebuttals: How much drug each patient got is the right question when nobody has measured it. Here it was measured, and it was fine.
Raising the dose for everybody treats the answer as already known, and hands extra drug to the three in four who are getting better.
Different drugs are the response once you know what changed. Chosen now, it is a guess with a plan attached.

title: Where each measure acts
task: Match each aim to the measure that achieves it.
scene: The city wants something done, and the room is arguing as if only one thing can be chosen. Four proposals are on the table, and each acts at a different moment.
takeaway: Measures that act at different moments are stronger together than more of any one of them.
why: Each of these acts at a different moment, which is why they add up instead of competing. Stopping the germ getting into a cell has to happen before it does. Calming the damage happens afterwards, and giving it too early gets in the way of a defence still doing its job.

choices: Something that blocks the landing site, given before it arrives.
Treatment that calms the damage, timed carefully.
Vaccination.
Ventilation, distance and staying home when ill.
rebuttals: Blocking the landing site is a job for something that gets in the way of it, and it has to be there before the germ is.
Calming the damage is treatment after the fact, and timing decides everything. Too early and it holds back a defence still needed.
Having defences ready before exposure is what vaccination does. Arriving first is the whole point of it.
Ventilation and distance act on the passing on rather than on any patient, which is why they work whatever this turns out to be.
scenarios: Stop it getting into cells in the first place.
Cut short the damage after somebody is already ill.
Have defences ready before anybody meets it.
Give it fewer chances to pass between people.

title: From a promising result to a fair trial
task: Put the four steps in order.
scene: Two things look promising in the dish, and the city wants one of them in patients within the month. Neither has been tried in an animal, and the plan on the table says nothing about when to stop.
takeaway: Being in a hurry changes how fast the steps go, not which steps there are.
why: Being in a hurry changes the speed of this and not its shape. Knowing what the thing is supposed to do comes first, because otherwise there is nothing to test it against.

rebuttals: What it is supposed to do comes first. Without that there is nothing to test it against except hope.
Animals and laboratory work second. A thing that harms an animal has told you something you needed before a person took it.
What counts as working, and when to stop, third. Chosen after the results arrive, they can be chosen to suit.
The watched trial last. It is what everything before it exists to make fair.
cards: Say what it is supposed to do, and how.
Show it works, and find the obvious harms, first.
Write who is in it, what working means, and when to stop.
Run the trial, watched by people who are not running it.

title: Three slots, six good ideas
task: Spend the three slots so the response does not fail all at once.
scene: Dr. Nia Okafor has six workable ideas and three slots to fund. Some can work this month. Others take longer, and some fail for exactly the same reasons as each other.
question: Which three keep the response working if one assumption turns out wrong?
takeaway: A set of measures is stronger when they do not all depend on the same thing going right.
why: Layers are only layers if they fail separately. Ventilation lowers the chance of catching it. It does not wait for anybody to be found. Fast isolation works after somebody is found, and cuts what happens next. A vaccine takes longer, and protects a different way.
answerText: Ventilation, fast isolation and the vaccine. Two act this month by different routes, and the third adds a different kind of protection later.

title: What each claim has earned
task: Spend the two checks on the claims that need them most.
scene: The emergency is closing, and four signed claims are going into the city's record. Two checks are left. The evidence under the four is not equally strong.
question: Which claims need checking before the report can say them at full strength?
takeaway: Say each claim at the strength its own evidence can carry.
why: A report should not give everything the same confidence. How it spreads is backed by three separate streams, so it can carry planning. Who gets sickest comes from one small group of patients, and it is about to become city policy.
answerText: Check who gets sickest, and how long the treatment holds. The rest is either backed already or written as still open.

title: Build the public explanation
task: Order the briefing by how much each claim can carry.
scene: The mayor goes live in an hour. How it spreads is settled. The animal question is not. The treatment has eight weeks behind it. Every sentence will be replayed for years.
takeaway: A public account is ordered by the strength of its evidence, not by the order the work happened in.
why: Order it by what the evidence carries, strongest first. That is the order in which a listener can tell one kind of claim from another. Say the animal question as firmly as the spreading and the whole thing falls apart the day the animal turns out to be somewhere else.

cards: How it spreads, which three separate streams agree on.
Who gets sickest, which one small group of patients suggests.
Where it came from, which is still open.
What would settle each open question, and when.

title: What survives the emergency
task: Make the outbreak-response call before the next case report arrives.
scene: The emergency budget ends in three weeks, and anything not protected stops with it. Four programmes want the last line. The council votes this month.
question: Which capability should the city protect when the emergency budget closes?
takeaway: Keep the system that spots the next one, not the instrument that starred in this one.
why: Each stream sees a different part of an outbreak, and each is much less useful alone. Sequencing says what changed, and it needs samples that stand for the town. Sewage gives the earliest warning, and it names nobody and explains nothing. Hospital numbers say who is ill, and they arrive late.
answerText: The three streams together, with somebody funded to read them side by side. Any one of them alone is much less than what worked this time.

choices: The three streams together, with shared records and somebody to read them.
The sequencing bench, since it found the change.
The sewage sampling, since it gave the earliest warning.
None. Stop the outbreak programme, and rebuild when the next one starts.
rebuttals: Sequencing is powerful, and it needs samples that stand for the town, and it cannot say who is ill.
Sewage warns early, and it names nobody and cannot say what the illness does.
Throwing the records away removes the baselines that make the next signal readable at all.
